plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic array of circles arranged in six vertical columns, with arrows drawn among them and part of the field sitting on a gray background. Five columns hold five circles each, evenly stacked from top to bottom, while the rightmost column holds only three. In every full column the circle in the middle position is an open white disk and the remaining circles are filled solid black. The white disk in the third column from the left carries the italic label x. Straight vertical arrows within each full column run upward from lower circles to the middle disk and from that disk to the circle above, and long curved arrows arc from a column's bottom circle to its topmost one. Along the row of white disks, horizontal arrows point inward toward x: the disks in the fourth through sixth columns send arrows leftward into x, with farther ones curving above intervening columns, and x in turn sends arrows leftward to the disks in the second and first columns. A rounded gray region with stepped edges covers the two circles below x in its own column together with the white disk and every circle beneath it in each column to the right. Because each arrow encodes an ordering between two elements, the shaded block gathers the elements the arrow chains place on one side of x, turning a counting argument about the quality of a partition into a visible area.

elements: 28 circular nodes arranged in a grid of 6 columns and 5 rows. Columns 1-5 have 5 nodes each (rows 1-5), column 6 has 3 nodes (aligned with rows 2-4)
Median nodes in each column (row 3) with a white fill and black outline
All other nodes with solid black fill
Label 'x' adjacent to the median node in column 3
Straight vertical arrows connecting adjacent nodes within each column, pointing upwards to indicate sorted order
Long curved vertical arrows bowing leftward, connecting the bottom-most node to the top-most node in each column
Horizontal straight arrows connecting the row 3 median nodes: col 4 to 3, and col 3 to 2
Horizontal curved arrows bowing upwards connecting medians: col 5 to 3, col 6 to 3, and col 3 to 1
Gray shaded region (stepped blob) for 'Known Greater' covering the nodes below x in col 3, and all nodes in cols 4, 5, 6 at or below the median row (explicitly excluding x itself)
Alternative gray shaded region for 'Known Less' covering the nodes above x in col 3, and all nodes in cols 1 and 2 at or above the median row (explicitly excluding x itself)

interactions.label: Proof Phase
interactions.teaches: Builds the counting argument step-by-step: partitioning the array, finding local medians, finding the global median (x), and finally deducing the block of elements guaranteed to be greater than x.

interactions.label: Known Elements
interactions.teaches: Switches the counting block between elements guaranteed > x (bottom right) and elements guaranteed < x (top left), visually demonstrating that x bounds a constant fraction of the array on both sides.

Clicking x highlights the explicit transitive arrow chains (e.g., from a bottom-right element up to its group median, then across to x) that mathematically guarantee these elements are greater than x without direct comparison to it.

demo_steps.title: Divide into groups
demo_steps.narration: To find a good pivot, the SELECT algorithm first divides the n elements into groups of 5.

demo_steps.title: Find local medians
demo_steps.narration: We find the median of each group (white circles). The elements within each group are conceptually sorted, indicated by the vertical upward arrows.

demo_steps.title: Median of medians (x)
demo_steps.narration: We recursively find the median of these local medians, labeled x. The horizontal arrows show x's position relative to the other group medians.

demo_steps.title: Elements greater than x
demo_steps.narration: Because x is greater than half the medians, and each of those medians is greater than half its group, all elements in the shaded bottom-right region are strictly greater than x.

demo_steps.title: Elements less than x
demo_steps.narration: By symmetry, the elements in the top-left region are mathematically guaranteed to be less than x. This proves x acts as a well-centered pivot.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: 2D layout in XY plane. Node coordinates: Columns X=1 to 6 (spacing 2 units, X spans 2 to 12). Rows Y=1 to 5 (spacing 2 units, Y spans -2 to -10, top to bottom). Circles radius 0.35. Median nodes are at Y=-6. Col 6 has nodes only at Y=-4, -6, -8. Colors: nodes #000000, median nodes #ffffff with 2px black border. Shaded regions: Z=-0.5, #c0c0c0, drawn as a smoothed polygon covering the specified nodes with ~0.8 units padding, intentionally bypassing x so the pivot is outside the shaded area. Arrows: black, thin curves/lines with standard triangular heads. Straight vertical arrows connect adjacent nodes in a column. Curved vertical arrows use quadratic bezier curves bowing leftwards, connecting Y=-10 to Y=-2 (for cols 1-5) and Y=-8 to Y=-4 (for col 6). Horizontal curved arrows bow upwards. The click interaction brightens highlighted arrow chains to red (#ff0000).
interactionPlan.notes: Since this is a flat 2D diagram, axis_screen_angles is null. Use THREE.Line or Path for arrows, with an arrowhead cone at the terminus. The states in proofPhase progressively unhide elements: Elements -> Nodes only; Groups -> Add column spacing/visual grouping; Medians -> Medians turn white, add vertical arrows; Median of Medians -> Add horizontal arrows and x label; Counting Area -> Add shaded region. The toggle regionSelect flips the shaded area geometry to the opposite quadrant.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Button for stepping through SELECT's proof phases: group into fives, mark group medians, choose x, then shade elements known greater than x; each press adds only the next visual layer, making the counting argument build deliberately.
- Click x to highlight all arrow chains that certify comparisons to the median-of-medians; the affected circles and arrows brighten, showing why elements on one side of x can be counted without direct comparison to every item.
- Toggle between known-greater and known-less regions; the shaded block switches sides of x, making the symmetric partition guarantee visible for both halves of the proof.

authoredContext: We now examine a selection algorithm whose running time is O.n/ in the worst case. Like RANDOMIZED-SELECT, the algorithm SELECT finds the desired element by recursively partitioning the input array. Here, however, we guarantee a good split upon partitioning the array. SELECT uses the deterministic partitioning algorithm PARTITION from quicksort (see Section 7.1), but modified to take the element to partition around as an input parameter. The SELECT algorithm determines the ith smallest of an input array of n > 1 distinct elements by executing the following steps. (If n D 1, then SELECT merely returns its only input value as the ith smallest.) 1. Divide the n elements of the input array into bn=5c groups of 5 elements each and at most one group made up of the remaining n mod 5 elements. 2. Find the median of each of the dn=5e groups by first insertion-sorting the elements of each group (of which there are at most 5) and then picking the median from the sorted list of group elements. 3. Use SELECT recursively to find the median x of the dn=5e medians found in step 2. (If there are an even number of medians, then by our convention, x is the lower median.) 4. Partition the input array around the median-of-medians x using the modified version of PARTITION. Let k be one more than the number of elements on the low side of the partition, so that x is the kth smallest element and there are nk elements on the high side of the partition. 5. If i D k, then return x. Otherwise, use SELECT recursively to find the ith smallest element on the low side if i < k, or the .i k/th smallest element on the high side if i > k. To analyze the running time of SELECT, we first determine a lower bound on the number of elements that are greater than the partitioning element x. Figure 9.1 helps us to visualize this bookkeeping.
